opus-5.5.text:
I think the value of users is often misunderstood. Many people assume the main benefit is data, that more users means more tokens you can train on. That's part of it, but I don't think it's the most important part.

The most important thing users give you is a signal about what actually matters. When you're doing research in isolation, you optimize for benchmarks, and benchmarks are a very lossy proxy for real intelligence or real usefulness. Once real people are using the product, you start to see where the model fails in ways no benchmark captured: a long document it can't really reason over, a multi-step task where it loses track halfway, or an answer that's technically correct but not what the person needed. That tells you where to put your research effort.

The second thing is that it closes the loop. In the past, AI development was very linear: train a model, evaluate it, publish it. Now it's more of a cycle. You ship, you observe behavior, you form hypotheses about capability gaps, you go back and change the data recipe or the training objective, and you ship again. The faster that loop runs, the faster the model improves. A user base is what makes the loop spin.

But I'd add a caveat. Users don't directly tell you how to get to the next level of intelligence. If you only follow user feedback, you end up with incremental product polish. Fundamental capability jumps, like better reasoning, longer context, or agentic ability, often come from a technical conviction you have before users ask for it. So the way I see it, the user base is a compass and an accelerator, but it can't replace the research vision. You need both: a belief about where intelligence is going, and real-world usage to keep you honest along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says user behavior shows where the model fails and what matters, but does not state that it reveals the distribution of demand for the model.

r002.rationale: It describes using observed failures to guide research effort and changes to training, but does not say those observations are translated into model evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it helps in a few layers, and they're not all equally obvious.

The most direct one is data, but not in the way people usually mean. It's not that users generate tokens you train on. It's that users tell you where the model is actually failing. When you're building a model in the lab, you evaluate it on benchmarks, and benchmarks are a proxy. They're a compressed, biased sample of what people want. Once you have real users, the distribution of tasks is the real distribution. You see the long tail. You see things like, a user pastes in a 200-page PDF and asks a question about a table on page 137, and your model confidently makes something up. No benchmark would have told you that was the number one complaint. So the user base is a much better loss function than any leaderboard.

The second layer is that it changes how you prioritize research. We have a lot of ideas internally, and the question is always which ones matter. If you don't have users, you prioritize based on taste, or based on what's trending in papers. With users, you prioritize based on what moves the experience. For us, long context was partly a bet from first principles, but it was also very clearly something people were struggling with in practice. That kind of signal keeps the research honest.

The third layer is feedback for alignment and post-training. Preference data from real usage is much higher quality than preference data you collect from annotators who are reading a guideline. The annotator is guessing what a user wants. The user knows what they want. If you can design the product so that preference is expressed naturally, through regenerations, through follow-ups, through whether someone keeps going or gives up, you get a signal that's very hard to fake.

And then there's a fourth thing that's more subtle. Having users forces you to build the infrastructure for iteration. Deployment, monitoring, evaluation, fast release cycles. That infrastructure is itself a research asset. The teams that can go from an idea to a deployed change to a measured result in days will beat the teams that take months, even if the second team has better ideas on paper. So the user base is partly a forcing function for the organization to become a faster learner.

I'd also say there's a flip side. Users can pull you toward the local optimum. If you only optimize for what people complain about today, you end up polishing a model that's fundamentally limited. So you have to hold two things at once. Use the users to find the truth about where you are, but keep a research agenda that's about where the model should be in two years, which users can't tell you, because they can't imagine it yet.

r001.rationale: The response says real users reveal the real distribution of tasks and demand, including the long tail.

r002.rationale: It says users reveal where the model fails and that this is a better loss signal, but does not clearly describe turning those observations into model evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think having a user base gives you a much better sense of what actually matters. When you build a model, you have benchmarks, but those benchmarks don’t capture all the things people want to do. Users bring very diverse tasks, and you start to see where the model is useful and where it falls short.

That feedback helps you decide what to improve. For example, is the problem that the model doesn’t have the capability, or that it has the capability but can’t reliably follow the user’s instructions? Those require different solutions.

But having more users doesn’t automatically make the model better. You still need a process for turning that feedback into good evaluations and training signals, while respecting users’ privacy. I think the real advantage is a shorter loop between building something, seeing how people use it, and improving it.

r001.rationale: It says users bring diverse tasks and that observing them shows what people want to do and where the model is useful or falls short, communicating the demand distribution.

r002.rationale: It connects observations of where the model is useful or falls short to a process for turning user feedback into evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a user base helps you understand where the model actually falls short. Benchmarks can tell you some things, but users bring tasks and contexts that you might never think to test. You start to see which failures happen frequently and which improvements would really matter.

The challenge is turning that feedback into a useful signal. A user may dislike an answer because it’s wrong, because it misunderstood the question, or simply because the style isn’t what they wanted. Those are different problems. If you can understand the distinction, you can use that feedback to guide your evaluations and training, then see whether the next version actually works better for people.

r001.rationale: The response says users reveal unfamiliar tasks and frequent failures, but does not clearly state that they reveal the distribution of demand for the model.

r002.rationale: It says feedback can guide evaluations, but ties this mainly to distinguishing types of negative feedback; it does not clearly describe using observations of both user successes and struggles to build evaluations.
